analysis.one_liner: Creates a public federal database of police misconduct allegations and settlement costs.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Judiciary Committee, where it received no further action and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require federal law enforcement agencies to report police misconduct allegations, judgments, and settlements to the Justice Department, which would publish an annual summary and maintain a public, searchable online database. State and local governments receiving Byrne JAG grant money would have to report similar data or lose up to 10% of those funds. It also directs a Government Accountability Office study on the causes and costs of police misconduct.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people gain the ability to see, in one public place, how often misconduct allegations are made against police officers, what kinds of misconduct (use of force, wrongful death, false testimony, racial profiling), what personnel actions followed, and how much money—often from public budgets—goes to pay judgments and settlements. Communities affected by police misconduct get evidence to push for changes; taxpayers see where their money goes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents and taxpayers seeking police accountability

how_it_helps.text: Requires federal law enforcement agencies to report annual counts of misconduct allegations, judgments and settlements, the type of allegation (use of force, wrongful death, false testimony, racial profiling, sexual assault, and others), personnel actions taken, and the amount and source of money paid [S3].

Requires state and local governments that receive Byrne JAG grants to collect and report substantially similar data, with noncompliance costing them up to a 10% cut in those grant funds; missed funds are reallocated to governments that comply [S3].

Directs the Attorney General to create and maintain a public, searchable online database of all reported data and to issue annual press releases summarizing it, and directs GAO to study and report on the leading causes of misconduct judgments and which agencies spend the most on settlements [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies bear new record-keeping and reporting costs. State and local governments that decline to comply lose up to 10% of their Byrne JAG grant funds. Agencies also face public exposure of misconduct records they currently report nowhere in a standardized way.
analysis.who_pays_short: Law enforcement agencies; noncompliant grant recipients

drawbacks.text: The enforcement mechanism is weak: state and local agencies that ignore the reporting rules face only a maximum 10% cut of one grant program, so a government with little Byrne JAG funding could simply absorb the penalty, and the bill relies on self-reporting with the Attorney General merely verifying against public sources 'as practicable' [S3].

The bill collects data on allegations, not just substantiated findings, so agencies could argue the database paints officers with unproven accusations; the bill responds by excluding personally identifiable information about officers and preserving Privacy Act protections, but a complete picture would still depend on how DOJ presents the data [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a transparency measure, not a conduct mandate: it changes no police practices directly and spends no new money beyond administrative costs. Its value is giving the public a standardized national record of misconduct allegations and their financial cost, which today exists nowhere in one place. The main honest objection is that its only teeth—a small potential cut to one grant program—may not move governments that would rather keep the data dark.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tim Kaine introduced the Cost of Police Misconduct Act of 2021 in the Senate on March 2, 2021 [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary that same day; that was the final action in its history [S5].
The bill drew one cosponsor, a Democratic senator, and no further committee or floor action before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies and state and local governments keep reporting no standardized misconduct data; the public record of police misconduct costs remains as fragmented as before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Law enforcement agencies avoiding a misconduct database

for.name: Tim Kaine
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Cost of Police Misconduct Act of 2021 in the Senate and delivered introductory remarks [S1][S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, and with a single Democratic cosponsor and no recorded opposition, no partisan split was ever measured.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies (federal, state, and local)
industries.note: The bill would force agencies to compile and publish standardized records of misconduct allegations, settlements, and the personnel actions taken, data most agencies do not currently publish in any comparable form. It also penalizes noncompliant grant recipients with up to a 10% Byrne JAG cut.

industries.industry: Municipal insurers and local government risk pools
industries.note: Governments would have to disclose whether settlements were paid from liability insurance, bonds, or general budgets, exposing how misconduct costs are financed. Taxpayers ultimately bear many of these costs, so public visibility runs with the public's interest.
